Where is Putin’s bunker located? Vladimir Putin has multiple bunkers — on this photo, his residence in Altai (which went on fire yesterday), where one of such bunkers is located. Reportedly, Putin’s Altai nuclear bunker is built in the side of a mountain in Ongudai district and is supposed to be able to hold thousands of people. The nearby residence is officially registered as Gazprom sanatorium, but guarded by the presidential security guards. Vladimir Putin brought the Italian Prime Minister Berlusconi here in 2015. The construction of the residence cost 3 billion ruble (USD $136 million in 2009 money). The cost of the bunker will be many times higher. In 2011, “Autoreview” journalists, as part of a joint investigation with “Novaya Gazeta”, tried to get into the sanatorium, but the security turned them away, citing the special status of the facility intended for the country's top officials. Ongudai district in Altai region is located near the Russian border with Kazakhstan, China and Mongolia. Putin stayed at this “sanatorium” many times during unofficial visits to the Altai Mountains, so it’s safe to say, no one else would be allowed to “recuperate” there, knowing the level of paranoia of the Kremlin usurper. Presumably, every Putin’s residence has a bunker big enough to accommodate a team of hundreds, if not thousands. It’s believed that Putin has about 20 residences in Russia built for his exclusive use. A recent leak of the map showing top secret locations that the ministry of defence contractors connected to high-speed internet by fiber-optic cable might be showing all of them. And this means, Putin is probably already busy building new bunkers, hoping to outsmart Americans and find a safe place to hide where he wouldn’t be found.

Do Russians prefer Marine Le Pen over Emmanuel Macron in the upcoming French presidential election? Just 8 days ago, Russia’s RIA Novosti was gleefully celebrating, “Marine Le Pen buried Emmanuel Macron.” Last night, the Russian news were at a loss, not knowing how to comment on the fact that Marine Le Pen’s party lost not only to Macron’s centric alliance, but got beaten by the leftist “Popular Front”. The Kremlin didn’t prepare instructions for propagandists for such a case. But it was fixed overnight, and the Kremlin spin sounds as “France is finished”. In Kremlin’s version, it’s not Marine Le Pen that is “finished”, but the whole big country of France. Kremlin propagandists accused Macron in disregarding “the expression of the people’s will” — yes, this comes from the country where any opinion against the government gets you either in jail or grave — depending on Putin’s mood in the morning. An interesting background on Marine Le Pen is that her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, was a co-founder of the far-right party she was representing in the last 2 French presidential elections. The “National Front” party, which initially included Nazi-era collaborators, had been convicted multiple times for antisemitic hate speech and described the Holocaust as “a detail” of WWII history. However, in 2002, Le Pen Senior advanced into the 2nd round of presidential stand off against Jacques Chirac. That was the moment in French electoral history where the terrified French voters said, “Non!”, overwhelmingly rejecting Le Pen, with even the fans of the left voting to put Chirac, a conservative, in the Elysee Palace. Since then, French political parties used the tactic consistently against the far-right. The same strategy helped to consolidate centrist and leftist voters in the July 7 snap parliamentary elections, when Le Pen’s party only scored the 3rd, behind the leftist coalition and Macron’s alliance. Marine Le Pen’s father, who is now 96, left the big politics 13 years ago, in 2011. His party never won presidential elections. Following in his footsteps, Marine Le Pen participated in 2012, 2017 and 2022 presidential elections, losing them all. After her loss in 2022 presidential elections, Marine Le Pen handed the leadership to 26-year-old Jordan Bardella. He became the first person without the Le Pen name to lead the “National Front” since its founding in 1972. On the campaign trail, Le Pen and Bardella have presented themselves as “running mates”, with Le Pen vying for the presidency while pushing her protege for the position of prime minister. Obviously, Russian propagandists didn’t see Bardella as a proper leader, continuing to refer to Marine Le Pen as the leading force in the party. Yes, the leaders of the Russian regime are bitterly disappointed that Le Pen’s party didn’t win — they have already purchased expensive French champagne to celebrate (and its not a figure of speech — Google “Russians drink champagne for Donald Trump’s victory”). But they are hopeful that the leader of the leftist party that scored the majority of seats in the parliament will also interfere with France’s participation in NATO and especially with helping Ukraine. The hope expressed by pro-Putin commentators under the posts about Le Pen’s party loss is that “Melenchon will be even worse for Ukraine”, which means automatically, it will be better for Russia. 72-year-old Jean-Luc Mélenchon is a founder of left-wing ‘France Unbowed’ party. He became the self-appointed figurehead of the alliance comprised of — in addition to his own party — the Socialist Party, the French Communist Party as well as green, center-left and left-wing political groups, which scored the most number of seats in the parliamentary elections. The Russian propagandists keep their hopes up.

What are Vladimir Putin's ambitions in Ukraine, and what was he trying to accomplish there? On the first day of the war, February 24, 2022, Vladimir Putin announced the goals of the “special military operation” in Ukraine (Putin didn’t plan a long war). “I have made a decision to conduct a special military operation,” proudly proclaimed Putin. “Its goal is to protect people who have been subjected to abuse and genocide by the Kyiv regime for 8 years. And for this, we will strive for the demilitarization and denazification of Ukraine, as well as bringing to justice those who committed numerous bloody crimes against civilians, including citizens of the Russian Federation,” arrogantly recited Putin. “At the same time, our plans do not include the occupation of Ukrainian territories. We are not going to force anything on anyone,” insisted Putin. So, the stated goals were: That speech didn’t age well, did it? Putin was absolutely sure that his troops will face no resistance and they can just roll in, all the way to Kyiv. None of the 4 stated goals has been achieved; the 2 promises of “no occupation” and “no use of force” had proven to be total lies. If Putin’s goal was to prevent NATO expansion (in his speech on February 24, 2022, he whined for 10 minutes about it, before announcing, “I made a decision to conduct a special military operation”) — this, too, was a total failure, with Finland and Sweden joining NATO after Putin began the war. But the most indicative are the posts of Putin’s shills such as convicted child sex offender Scott Ritter, from March 2022 (1 month into the war): 2 days after this post, Russians began withdrawing from north Ukraine as a result of their total failure at Kyiv, Sumy, and Chernihiv. Altogether in 2022, Ukrainian armed forces de-occupied (liberated) over 50% of the territories captured by Russia in the first weeks of the invasion, after Russian troops treacherously attacked their “brotherly neighbor”. Russia utterly failed to reach its initial military and political objectives, set by Putin on February 24, 2022. Ukraine remains a sovereign country and this means, Putin isn’t winning by any means.

If Vladimir Putin learned he only had a few weeks to live, would he nuke the USA? Absolutely not: Vladimir Putin is a paranoidal sadist, but he’s certainly not seeking to destroy his life’s work and die a terrible death. If anything, he’s “a family man” and since recently have been bringing his 2 official daughters, a niece and a nephew closer, appointing them into the most important for him positions of power. He also has grandkids and spoke lovingly about them in the past. Since recently, Putin brought his daughters Maria and Katerina into the limelight. More than anything, a tale-telling sign is that Kremlin bots hysterically scream that “Putin will press the button if he is in a desperate situation.” There are more facts that point to Putin’s not being in a position to order a nuclear strike on the USA: Remember, Putin lives in isolation from the real world. He is watching the Russian TV where “experts”, including sold-out Americans — and even Ukrainians, assure the viewer of the “inevitable victory for Russia” in its war in Ukraine. His second source of information are the infamous red folders with printouts, carefully curated by his subordinates, none of whom wishes to be the bearer of bad news. So, from one hand, Putin cannot be confident that his order to nuke America would be fulfilled, and from the other hand, he is unsure if the Russian weapons can even hit the American soil successfully. But he can be confident that the responding strike will destroy everything he has been building for 25 years in Russia — and likely will end the Russian statehood. In his wish for historical immortality (which was the reason why Putin started the whole “USSR V.2” project), Putin will most certainly choose the path that gives him (in his view) a high probability of a long-term success of that project — and also allows him to spend his last days surrounded by the loving family and friends, with the best medical help available, passing away peacefully — as opposed to spending his last days in an underground bunker, where he is likely to suffer a terrible death being tortured by his own military (I’m convinced that Putin won’t be able to maintain control over his security forces if locked in an underground bunker — and knowing Putin’s level of paranoia, he must understand it as well). Putin started the war in Ukraine, being delusional, but it’s his dedication to the neo-USSR project that is the safety switch against Putin’s giving an order to nuke the USA.

How is the Russian economy doing? What kind of data has its economy produced in recent months, positive or negative? From January 2020 to May 2024, inflation in Russia is double the G7 average. Russia’s central bank had to raise its base interest rate from 7.5% in June 2023 to 16% in June 2024 — and in July 2024, it was increased by 200 basis points at once — to 18% per annum. So, Russia’s base interest rate is 3% higher than in Afghanistan. There are no plans to reduce the key rate this year, stated Elvira Nabiullina, head of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation. She added that the rate will remain high for a long time, and an additional increase is possible. Thank the glorious leader Vladimir Putin for that. Meanwhile, a Russian economist who was explaining how badly Russia was doing just “accidentally fell out of a window”. Another unfortunate accident amidst the epidemic of high-rise falls of state execs in the Russian capital. Russia is doing just fine — even great, insisted Vladimir Putin in his recent speech in the Kremlin, promising that the economy of the occupied Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Donetsk and Luhansk regions will be by 2030 on the level of “the rest of Russia”. (Video in the comments below.) If anyone saw the devastation of “the rest of Russia”, this certainly sounds like a threat rather than an optimistic forecast. And it’s highly doubtful that Russia is capable to quickly bring back to life the destroyed Ukrainian cities. Mariupol, Bakhmut, Avdeevka, Marinka — these Ukrainian cities had their own thriving identities before the war — Russia put on them the mangled masks of the “Russian world.” The ruins are visible on Google Planet, from satellites. In the past weeks, Russia got hit by rolling blackouts — in Krasnodar region, people went to the streets to protest, after not having power and water for several days — the water supply was switched off because there was no power. There are rumors of an accident at a nuclear power station near Rostov, and as a result, insufficient power produced to supply the nearby regions. The “new regions” — how Putin calls the occupied Ukrainian territories — are getting the power from Russia; before the occupation, they were getting the electricity from Ukraine. The Russian grid hadn’t been maintained and repaired properly due to the lack of funds (the money is spent on the war in Ukraine) and western sanctions (parts aren’t easily accessible — and Russia doesn’t make them). Russia is stuck in Ukraine and the money is disappearing in the black hole of the war, with nothing but ruined cities to show for that. And these ruined cities will require an enormous investment to bring them back to life — and who’s going to invest in a territory that’s occupied and can change its citizenship or be bombed to ruins tomorrow? “Russians will have many more troubles because the country is worn out. It was necessary to close Russia down for the major renovation for about 10 years. Then it would’ve been possible to live through the 21st century normally. Instead of that, the country was sent to war,” says Igor Lipsits, a prominent Russian economist and founder of the Higher School of Economics in Moscow, who was forced to emigrate because of his critical stance. The Russian economy is in a state of flux. The western sanctions suffocate it slowly but surely — and this is why Putin keeps demanding the lifting of western sanctions as a condition of a “peace agreement”. Because Russia is screwed unless the sanctions are lifted — no matter what is the situation on the ground in Ukraine. There is really no good scenario for the Russian economy — its down spiral is irreversible at this point. It’s like a worn off car — it requires a complete rebuild to operate properly again.

Russian military bloggers say that Ukrainian forces broke through defenses in Belgorod region — that’s the second Russian region getting invaded. Meanwhile, Russian volunteers who arrived to Kursk region with “humanitarian aid” for the Russian army (food, water, socks and jocks for soldiers, because the Russian army doesn’t provide for its troops — officers steal all the money) — so, these “volunteers” complain about traffic police cameras, which continue to send them tickets for speeding — while they are driving over the speed limits to avoid drones or shelling. The traffic police office responded that “war is war, but a violation is a violation” and fines that have already been issued in the system can only be challenged in court. You know, in Russia the law is the law! (Unless, of course, you are above the law, in which case you can break any laws you want.) On day 3, the chief of Russian general staff Gerasimov reported to Putin that the enemy had been repelled and destroyed. That was more than 3 weeks ago. Ukrainians are still in the Kursk region and keep increasing their stronghold. And now , Russians are told by their TV channels that "The incursion into Kursk region by the Ukrainians is beneficial to Russia, because it closes the conversations about negotiations with Ukraine.” Putin hopes that “the situation” in the Kursk region will somehow sort itself out, so he tries not to make a big deal about “mighty Russia” getting invaded by a “little, insignificant Ukraine.” Being invaded by a foreign power is Russia’s “new normal”.

Why does the current Russian military seem so incompetent? The current Russian military doesn’t just seem incompetent — they are incompetent. And corrupt — from top to bottom. A Russian contract soldier who deserted and escaped to the West told about the disarray and corruption in the Russian army to Verstka Media. Anton (not his real name) decided to sign a contract with the Russian army to pay off the debts. Anton was struggling to repay loans amounting to 1 million ruble ($10,000). In Russia, most people don’t earn such money in a year. It were the bailiffs who convinced Anton to sign up for the war in Ukraine. Ads for army contract service are plastered all over Russia. (Stock photos are used throughout this post.) The conditions they offered sounded great: a contract with the civil organization JSC Investinform (it gets paid for recruiting soldiers for the war with Ukraine), plus the regional payout on sign up, plus payments from the Ministry of Defense. In total, Anton was supposed to be earning about 350,000 rub. per month ($3,500). In August 2023, Anton arrived in Moscow, signed a 1-year contract with the Ministry of Defense and an employment contract with JSC Investinform. The second contract allowed him to get top-up payments in addition to the standard 215,000 rub. ($2,150) MOD wage to Russian soldiers in Ukraine. That’s how Moscow officials meet the allocated quotas of soldiers per region: on paper, these recruits are Muscovites, but in reality, it’s deprived residents of small Russian towns living in poverty that are sent to the war. Muscovites have no desire to die for Putin; they live quite well. Think ‘Hunger Games’ districts and the Capitol: that’s Russia and Moscow. On sign up, Anton was immediately paid 400,000 rub. ($4,000). All debt collection proceedings against him had been suspended — that’s another “perk” offered to desperate Russians in need, to convince them to sign up for the war. However, he couldn’t use the money to repay the debts. Instead, he was forced to spend the money he got upfront to buy a proper uniform and personal protective equipment — bulletproof helmet, vest, etc. When new recruits arrived to the army training grounds, they were given some ancient uniforms and combat boots — all of them were 4–6 sizes too large. The helmet was from the times of WWII, a piece of shrapnel would pierce it like paper. But as soon as they arrived to barracks, helpful “intermediates” arrived, eager to sell to the fresh recruits all they needed. Nothing in the Russian army was for free. If you came to “earn big money”, you first needed to buy your own gear. The newbies had to pay the full retail price for their clothing and equipment. On top of that, they had to pay for parts for the machinery they would be using in the future. Some lame excuse was offered to make them pay for parts. Basically, commanders know how much cash you have been just paid, and extract it all before you have a chance to spend it. $4,000 went quick. The workers of the military warehouse where they were supposed to get equipment and uniforms were all drunk. Half of the officers were drunk as well. Quickly the recruits learned that they had to buy not only their own military gear but also food: within 2 weeks, all soldiers got food poisoning from eating the meals in the military canteen. So, they had to buy food in the local kiosk, where a liter of milk cost $8. The shop assistant was driving a luxury Mercedes, Anton says. Corruption in the Russian army is all-permeating. Because of Anton’s vocal complaints about the equipment, he was sent to a “Storm-Z” unit after the training course. Storm-Z is the “penal brigades”, where murderers and robbers recruited from prisons and deserters who were caught are shipped. Out of 600 recruits delivered to the front with him, only 40 survived after 2 months of assaults near Kupyansk. “It was just some kind of extermination. From one company, 5–6 people would return alive. The tanks and armored carriers were also smashed. In the end, we were mixed with prisoners and were simply pushed, pushed, pushed ahead.” How did he survive? “How I survived is a good question. I was a grenade launcher, not a stormtrooper, I didn’t go in attacks. We operated from hidden positions. Direct fire in these fields is not an option,” recalls Anton. “In 9 cases out of 10, storm troops are liquidated on approach.” “There are no experienced people in the infantry; people run away. If a person survives, he refuses to go on attacks, he starts having anxiety and hysterics. People rather go to jail than go on attacks.” In the village of Zaytsevo (Luhansk region), there is an unofficial jail where the Russians are holding soldiers who refused to continue to fight. Some of them say it’s “hell”, but it surely beats dying under heavy artillery fire trying to storm fortified Ukrainian positions. “The losses were simply insane, I lost count. For 3 kilometers, which were eventually taken back by the Ukrainians, 5–6 companies were killed,” According to Anton, the commanders are reprimanded for heavy losses, so all of those who haven’t returned from the attack are reported as “missing” (presumed deserters), not killed. Anton was deployed from the beginning of October till the end of November 2023. By that time, only a few people were left in his unit. They were taken in the rear of Russia-occupied Luhansk region, where they had to train the new recruits — prisoners and contractors. Then suddenly they were loaded on trucks and shipped to a camp in the Belgorod region (Russian territory near the border with Kharkiv region of Ukraine). By mid-March 2024, they were sent on the location near the Ukrainian border. Their unit was loaded on trucks (most Russian armed personnel carriers are destroyed by now, the troops are moved around by trucks) and for the whole night and the next day their column was driving on roads. Anton didn’t know that a raid by “Freedom of Russia Legion” was ongoing in the Belgorod region for already 3 days. He says that their commanders also didn’t know what was going on. Their trucks got under artillery fire. One of Anton’s colleagues was killed in a strike. His group hid at a cottage of a 90-year-old granny. No one knew what to do, commanders didn’t give any orders. They were under fire for several hours. Only the next morning the commanders contacted them and told them where to go. By that time, all locals escaped the village, stores and offices didn’t operate. The soldiers were ordered to stay in the local school, which was also closed. The soldiers simply hid there and slept. Communication with the base wasn’t working. They were under artillery fire, drones circling above the place. “We heard the conversations of our comrades, but we could not answer. There was an attack and breakthrough at their positions. Not only Storm-Z units were there but also border guards. In the meantime, it turned out that a whole platoon had been demolished in the woods.” Later the same day Anton went with a group to evacuate the wounded and dead from the battlefield — he had to replace the deceased colleague, although he hadn’t done evacuations before. During the evacuation, the group had to shed their weapons and armor, which weighed up to 50 kg, and walked 5 km back to the school. (The wounded guy that Anton evacuated died in the hospital.) In the basement, where the school canteen was, they took some sleep. As they woke up, they had to go back to get their weapons. Anton marked the location where he hid his grenade launcher on the map with an asterisk. “If I lost the grenade launcher, I would be transferred to the infantry, and infantry means certain death. Machine guns and rifles are dime a dozen, but it’s nearly impossible to procure something mightier.” Anton says that once his commander opened up and blurted: “I don’t give a f**k about you contractors, they’ll send me as many of you as I need — but for the lost equipment I would be hauled over the coals, it’s a lot of paperwork.” In storm troops, losses reach up to 90%, says Anton. He believes that if it weren’t for aerial bombing by the Russian Air Forces, the units of Russians that are fighting for Ukraine (“Freedom of Russia” Legion and the Russian Volunteer Corps, who were responsible for the raid on the Russian territory) would have easily captured the border areas of the Belgorod region with the help of FPV drones and artillery. Ukraine is superior to Russia by half a century in technical terms, their artillery is more accurate, and drones constantly conduct reconnaissance, Anton says. After the raid, the commander of Anton’s unit went on a drinking binge — along with his entire headquarters. The commander blamed the signalman for the failure in communications and began beating him up — after a few days of the torture, the signalman deserted. Meanwhile, Anton himself was thinking about doing the same thing. At the end of March 2024, he was watching a video of Russian oppositional channel ‘TV Dozhd’ (they were banned in Russia in 2022 and now broadcast from Europe), which mentioned the organization that helped Russian soldiers to escape the army and desert from the front (‘Idite Lesom’). At first he was skeptical, but when rumors about an upcoming offensive in the Kharkiv region spread, decided to give it a go. Anton says he realized that it’s impossible to survive in the Russian storm troops. Before agreeing to sign the contract, he had completely different ideas what it would be like. He asked the commanders to take 3 days off, but they refused. He couldn’t get a leave either — he says that even mobilized soldiers who serve since September 2022 can’t get a vacation. But he managed to get commanders’ permission to leave the unit for 1 night — until the morning. “Almost everyone who has been behind the front line thinks about escaping,” says Anton. 1.5 months after his escape, he cannot adapt to the peaceful life in a safe European country. Sometimes he has panic attacks and adrenaline rushes, but he tries to suppress them. His attitude towards the war in Ukraine has changed greatly. “There is guilt on me,” admits Anton. ”Once, our detachment commander broke down, drunk: “Yes, we are f***ing orcs!” “It’s disillusionment. The commanders don’t show it, and such coming outs happen mainly because they are drunk. During my time there, my entire outlook on life changed. I no longer feel anything positive about the Russian state. This is not a war, but some kind of agony. The only parallels that emerge are with the World War 1. We are simply being sent to slaughter,” concludes Anton. He plans to stay in Europe and apply for political asylum. He believes that he has the right to claim it as “a person who refused to participate in war crimes.” He never fully repaid the loans — and has no plans to do it.

They also gave us mashed potatoes made from greenish potatoes, which were salad-colored.” “They also beat us during interrogations. I'm just a simple border guard, not an assault trooper, not a marine, not a machine gunner. And even then, I lost half of my teeth during these interrogations. What they did to the machine gunners or snipers is terrifying to imagine.” Oleksandr Hrytsiuk from Kivertsi, Volyn region, was captured in April 2022. In January 2024, his wife was informed that his body had been returned from captivity. When his wife arrived in Kyiv for body identification, she was shocked by what she saw. “It was a very horrifying sight. What struck me the most was how emaciated the body was.” The pathologist said that Oleksandr’s body weighed less than 50 kilograms. He was tall — 180 cm, and before captivity, he weighed 110 kg and was physically healthy. “What was left of him were just bones and skin. His head was all bruised, his nose was crooked, and his index fingers had no nails. Whether they were ripped out or smashed, I do not know. There were signs of torture all over his body,” his wife says. Some of his cellmates survived and later later told the story how they were tortured. Every day they were beaten — either in the cell or taken out of the cell to interrogation chambers. The Russians beat Ukrainian prisoners brutally, and Oleksandr was their prime target, because he was tall, he was from western Ukraine, and didn’t want to speak Russian. The guards barely fed them, sometimes even just threw them some dog food mixed with dog hair. “They called him a ‘Banderite’, saying all Banderites must be killed and cut to pieces. He was beaten very cruelly, to the point of losing consciousness. Between beatings, they were forced to stand motionless for hours, sometimes with their hands raised.” This is only a small part of Russian war crimes. There are many more details on terrifying conditions of Ukrainian POWs in Russian captivity. Please read and spread the word.

What would make people laugh at Putin? Putin’s claims about Russia’s economic “progress” are the butt of many jokes. Yesterday, at St. Petersburg’s international economic forum, Putin announced that Russia has already overtaken Japan and Germany in terms of the size of the economy, but it needs to ensure stable growth further. “Literally last week, the World Bank made additional calculations and put Russia in 4th place,” Putin announced proudly. “Russia has the fourth largest GDP in terms of purchasing power parity, as I said, ahead of Japan,” insisted Putin. I don’t know what numbers Rosstat supplies to the World Bank (the World Bank uses the official Russian statistics), but 80% of Russia looks like this: I don’t believe for a second that a Japanese worker earning the average wage can buy less food or things than someone earning the average wage in Russia. Maybe, only if they calculate how many loafs of bread one can buy (bread only), but not if you compare the actual needs of a person living a regular life. For Russians, the lifestyle of an average Japanese is the level of unaffordable luxury. Meanwhile, in the center of Moscow, on Bobrov Lane, an elevator fell out of a shaft. Just by pure luck, a person didn’t end up dead. Soon there could be many more such incidents. The Russian authorities decided to increase the service life of dilapidated lifts from 25 to 30 years. 70,000 elevators in Russia (Russia doesn’t produce lifts but had been buying them abroad all these years) are at the end of their service life. Maintenance is also an issue because of western sanctions. At the same time, the level of cajolery towards Putin is hitting record heights. At the SPIEF, the moderator of Putin’s Q&A session promoted him as a messiah whose job is “to save the world,” depicting his appointment in 1999 as an act of “God’s mercy” to Russia. Putin’s face was glowing with delight. If what Russia turned into by 2024 is an act of “God’s mercy”, I am scared to think what God’s wrath towards Russia would look like.

What do you think will happen as fighting rages on in Russia's Kursk region? A Russian soldier’s chevron proclaims, “Like it or not, but Russia is expanding,” echoing a popular folk adage. Ironically, the soldier was captured by the Ukrainian troops, expanding the zone of Ukraine’s occupation in Russia. (Video in the comments below.) In 18 days, Ukraine managed to capture around 1,300 square km in the heavily-populated region of Kursk in Central Russia. Ukraine invaded Russia on August 6, 2024, and for over 2 weeks, there is nothing that the Russian army can do to repel the surprise invasion of the “sacred Russian land.” Vice versus, the Ukrainian army keeps capturing 1–3 villages daily, and there are already 94 settlements under their control. The Ukrainian army established military administration on the occupied territories, to ensure order and manage humanitarian assistance to remaining residents: as many as 130,000 residents evacuated from the occupied towns to Russia (as reported by the Russian side), with around 20,000 Kursk region residents remaining on the Ukraine-controlled territory. There is also a curfew from 5 pm to 10 am, introduced by the Ukrainian military administration, giving residents only 7 hours during which they can get out of their homes. Initially, Russian leaders didn’t treat Ukraine’s incursion into the Kursk region seriously and ordered to use compulsory draftees aged 18–19 to plug the holes, instead of moving experienced units of contract soldiers from the territory of Ukraine. Now, reports are surfacing that units of the Russian army are starting to be moved, to be used on the territory of the Kursk Oblast, tasked with the goal of squeezing out the Ukrainian forces. This is opening the opportunity for the Ukrainian units standing against Russians in Ukraine to increase counterattacks on the territory of partially occupied Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Luhansk regions — and apparently, the Ukrainian forces are already using these gaps. We’ll hear more in the coming days. So, the Kursk operation is only a part of a bigger plan by the Ukrainian commander-in-chief to seize the initiative. Apparently, Ukrainians used a brand-new weapon to target the Voronezh site — a jet-powered drone ‘Palyanitsia’. Each of these strikes is a stroke of a global plan. We are not seeing isolated, random attempts at attacks. We are witnessing the implementation of carefully orchestrated series of operations within the framework of a single plan. What is the main goal of the plan? To force the Russian troops to leave Ukraine.

Why did Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán confirm to a pro-Putin journalist that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy did not back his "peace plan"? It’s very simple: Victor Orbán has no “peace plan”. Advisor to the Office of the President of Ukraine Mykhailo Podolyak stated: "An immediate ceasefire, leaving the occupied territory of Ukraine to Russia and sitting down at the negotiating table is not peace. This is what Russia needs to get away from the responsibility as such and saturate the war zone with resources.” Not that Orbán doesn’t understand it. He’s been in politics long enough to realize what Putin’s “peace proposal” entails. So, why is he working to advance Putin’s agenda? Because he bet on Putin’s victory — and is about to lose. And probably Putin’s goons explained to him what they are going to leak to the media if Orbán doesn’t do as required. Remember Orbán’s visit to Moscow on February 1, 2022 — 3 weeks before the invasion? I do. At the time, Orbán also described the visit as a "peace mission." However, no significant agreements were signed, so the true purpose of the visit remains unclear. So many questions remain unanswered. One thing for sure, Orbán is hiding the true reasons for his advocating for Ukraine’s surrender. And Ukraine’s interests are the last thing that Orbán is concerned about.

How did the myth of the mighty Russian Army start? In Nizhny Novgorod region, mobilized soldiers who were wounded are being handcuffed to a radiator in a decaying prison building. They get beaten and abused for refusing to go back to the front in Ukraine. (Video in the comments below.) Such treatment is supposed to motivate them to agree to go back to the war. At the front in Ukraine, “refuseniks” are casually shot; on the territory of Russia, they are abused and tortured by hunger, beaten, often raped. “The mighty Russian army” doesn’t exist. It never existed. There was the Soviet army, which was also built on fear, brainwashing and propaganda — but there was something else. The Soviet people who fought against Hitler troops in WWII — and prevailed, were fighting to repel the enemy and kick out the invaders from their land. This isn’t what the Russian army is doing in Ukraine — it’s not what the Russian army was doing in Georgia or Syria. No one invaded the Russian Federation since it became a country in 1991. “Every war is terrible, and the Russian-style war is ugly,” writes Mykhailo Podolyak, advisor to the office of the president of Ukraine. “Without a pity for your own and others, when destruction is preferred to capturing. The deserts scorched by Russian bombs on our land will take decades to heal. Some cities will not be rebuilt. Missile and bomb attacks on hospitals, rape of people regardless of gender and age, abduction of children, executions of prisoners and their own refuseniks – the real ‘Gerasimov Doctrine’ has turned crimes into a tactic of war,” says Podolyak. That’s the only way that the Russian army under Putin knows. They are unable to fight differently, the whole Russian army is one giant war crime. And that’s how they are trying to fight against Ukraine’s invasion in the Kursk region. “Now Putin's army is fighting on the territory of RF, shelling and storming Russian cities and towns. Russian pilots are destroying civilian infrastructure in the Kursk region with multi-kilogram bombs, forcing tens of thousands of local residents to leave their homes. Russian soldiers are looting shops and civilian homes of their neighbors,” describes Podolyak. Before, Russians were watching the war as a television show, but for hundreds of thousands of Kursk region residents, the war is now becoming close and personal. And they can feel and experience what the Ukrainian residents living near the border with Russia had been living through for years. This new reality terrifies them. As is the fact that “the mighty Russian army” can’t protect them.

When will the war in Ukraine stop? TAP ON THE PHOTO TO VIEW. According to the commander of Kadyrov's ‘Akhmat’ unit, Apti Alautdinov, the whole SMO will be over in 2–3 months. Apti films himself against a camo net on a blue wall, so it looks like he’s on the front line. For his own videos he also wears a helmet and a bulletproof vest, to appear tough — but for the interview to a Chinese channel, he decided to skip these. It looks totally comical knowing that ‘Akhmat’ troops don’t participate in fights — their job is to shoot the Russian soldiers who retreat when sent into an assault. In the Kursk region, Kadyrov’s guys who had been stationed there were looting and abusing locals, happy to be paid big money for doing not much — until the Ukrainian troops invaded, which no one in Russia expected. If they did expect it, ‘Akhmat’ fighters in USD$2000 hoodies wouldn’t be captured — they would retreat before that. ’Akhmat’ guys have explicit instructions to get out in case of any danger. “It’s not your war, guys. It’s the Russians’ war,” explained them their commanders. “You shouldn’t be dying for Russia.” Of course. Kadyrov positions himself to fight for power after Putin departs — he needs to save his loyal trained Chechen fighters for himself. On his way from Azerbaijan, Vladimir Putin visited Chechnya and talked to a group of selected ‘Akhmat’ fighters. Putin was sucking up to Kadyrov’s guys and cracking them up to the nines — it’s embarrassing even to watch. (Video in the comments below.) Putin hopes that Kadyrov's guys will protect and save him. He hopes he can buy their loyalty. Putin has very poor grasp of history. There was another interesting personage at that meeting. Remember that guy? On the right bottom is Vadim Krasikov, Putin’s personal killer, who was recently swapped for American journalist Evan Gershkovich and a bunch of Russian political prisoners. The guy behind the speaking Putin looks eerily alike him. Some said that a Putin’s double was sent to perform a PR tour, to show the public that the great strategist isn’t hiding in a bunker. The purpose of the visit to Chechnya was apparently to bargain with Kadyrov about fighting off the Ukrainian incursion in the Kursk region. Putin would probably gladly pay a few billion dollars to the person who can push out the Ukrainian troops from Russia. 2 years ago, Putin made a deal with Yevgeny Prigozhin that his ‘Wagner’ would capture Bakhmut. Prigozhin killed 20,000 of his men (mostly prisoners) in the “meat attacks” — but managed to take the town. Now Putin hopes to buy Kadyrov to do the same in the Kursk region. Only Kadyrov is not a fighter and not a strategist, and neither is Apti. And taking Bakhmut was an easier task than taking back 1,300 square kilometers and 93 settlements in the Kursk region. In fact, in today’s Russia, it would be easier for Kadyrov to overthrow Putin than to push the Ukrainian troops out of the Kursk Oblast. The pace of developments is speeding up in Russia. By the way, in 2 days – on August 23 – it’s a year since Putin killed Prigozhin. Feels like it happened in another life.

Are the Russian people ready for a nuclear war? The overwhelming majority of Russians (76%) do not support the use of nuclear weapons, even if it were required for Russia’s victory in the war, the latest survey of the ‘Russian Field’ research group revealed. Compared to 2023 poll, the number of those who are against of a nuclear strike increased by 2% (which is within the margin of statistical error). More often than others, men over the age of 60 were in favor of a nuclear strike. Most of them also think that starting a war in Ukraine was a good idea. World War 3 Russian propagandists promote this idea tirelessly, so by now 57% of Russians believe that WW3 is a real possibility. Who will Russia be fighting against in WW3? The weirdest thing is that only 12% of Russians see Ukraine as the enemy in that war. After sending hundreds of thousands of men to die in Ukraine for 2.5 years, Russians don’t list Ukraine among those Russia must fight against in a world war! Classic example of the Russian cognitive dissonance syndrome. At the same time, respondents named China (58%), Belarus (48%), Iran (21%) and North Korea (20%) as Russia’s main allies in a world war. Who will win the world war? As sociologists note, Russians without higher education, those on low-income and residents of small towns most often believe in Russia’s victory in a world war. Fact: Putin is winning the war for the minds of Russians. The survey showed that Russians’ trust in military propaganda increased: So, from one hand, most Russians say they believe the official version of the Russian state. However, even after 2.5 years of non-stop brainwashing, with any freedom of speech liquidated and any free media squashed, with dissenters locked in prisons for decades — even after that, 40% of Russian respondents admit that they do not trust that their government tells them the truth.

What is now left of Russia's Black Sea fleet? The last ships of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet left the occupied Crimea — it’s too unsafe for them under the Ukrainian missile strikes. Because Crimea is a Ukrainian territory, occupied by Russia, the U.S., U.K., France and other countries aiding Ukraine with weapons to defend itself have no limitations on the use of their weaponry to strike the whole territory of Crimea. And because Ukraine first destroyed the Russian anti-air defence systems, Russia faced huge problems trying to protect its troops and navy in Crimea. The Russian Black Sea Fleet lost almost a third of its ships due to Ukrainian attacks. The last large Russian patrol ship was forced to leave Crimea a week ago, said Dmytro Pletenchuk, speaker of the Ukrainian Naval Forces. Most Russian ships moved from Sevastopol to Novorossiysk, a port on the territory of Russia. “Our Black Sea Fleet fled from the battlefield, fled from Crimea! The reality is that our air defense is not able to cope with drones and missiles. This is a complete failure,” complained Russian colonel Viktor Alksnis (friend of Igor Girkin). Igor Girkin and Victor Alksnis. Girkin himself is enjoying the gratitude of Vladimir Putin for his service to Russia — including Girkin’s role in igniting the war in Donbas in 2014 — in a Russian prison. Putin ordered to lock him up, because Girkin was criticizing the war in Ukraine and predicting that Russia is heading for a catastrophe. Girkin was convicted for the crime of “extremism” — the same crime that many Russian opposition politicians have been locked up for.

Did Ukraine just test its first ballistic missile? Ukraine had the capability to build ballistic missiles since the times of the USSR, but after signing the Budapest memorandum in 1994, Ukraine had to dispose of its arsenal of carriers of strategic nuclear warheads. Ukraine also surrendered to Russia many missiles that Putin’s army used in attacks since February 2022. So, when president Zelenskyy announced on August 27, 2024, that Ukraine has successfully tested its new ballistic missile, it was something that many analysts expected for a long time. Ukrainian journalist Dmitry Gordon (left), who was a friend of former Ukrainian president Leonid Kuchma (right) described their conversation in 2006 when Kuchma told him that Ukraine had both the capability and expertise to build ballistic missiles. Kuchma also told Gordon that Ukraine was able to build “as many as necessary” ballistic missiles. Leonid Kuchma knew what he was talking about. He began working on ‘Yuzhmash’ aerospace plant in the Ukrainian city of Dnipropetrovsk in 1960, straight after graduation from a university as an engineer. On ‘Yuzhmash’, Kuchma was working in the design bureau, where the Soviet missile systems were created. Then he moved to the position of technical director of rocket tests at the Baikonur Cosmodrome — the #1 space rocket launching pad of the USSR. During his career, Kuchma worked as a chief of both legendary flagships of the Ukrainian rocket and space industry — ‘Yuzhmash’ aerospace plant and ‘Yuzhnoye’ design bureau. For his contribution to development of rocket engineering, Kuchma was awarded the Lenin Prize in 1979 (12 years before the dissolution of the USSR). After Kuchma became the 2nd president of independent Ukraine, the first Ukrainian satellite "Sich-1" was launched into space (1995). In an interview to BBC in June 2022, Kuchma said that the latest developments of Dnepropetrovsk aerospace engineers included analogues of western weapons that Ukraine had to beg western partners for: for example, missile systems with a range of hundreds of kilometers. So, the appearance of Ukrainian-made ballistic missiles was only a matter of time — and I think Putin knew it, this is why he was in such a hurry to pressure Ukraine to sign a “peace agreement” that would prohibit further development of Ukrainian weapons. But Putin underestimated both Ukraine and the West. And now his strategic loss is obvious to anyone keeping abreast of the latest developments in this war.

Why did Russia want Vadim Krasikov so badly to be part of the largest US-Russia prisoner swap? Vadim Krasikov is linked to Vladimir Putin since 1990s when he was stealing hundreds of millions of dollars with St. Petersburg’s mayor Anatoly Sobchak — Krasikov was a bodyguard for them, and obviously a silent witness to many shady deals. Putin’s judo trainer Leonid Usvyaytsov was part of St. Petersburg’s organized crime since the city was called Leningrad. It was Usvyaytsov who got teenage Putin into the law faculty of Leningrad State University under the sports quota. Reportedly, it was also Usvyaytsov who told young Vladimir to apply to the KGB to be an informer, which Putin became already at the university. Putin held Usvyaytsov in high regard and in his earlier years as the president of Russia spoke about him with utmost respect. It was Usvyaytsov who trained Putin in the framework of “understandings” (“ponyatia”) of “the thief’s code” of ethics, used in Russian criminals gangs and prisons — and now also among the Russian enforcers. Later all mentions of Leonid Usvyaytsov disappeared from the official Putin’s biography. Usvyaytsov crafted his poetic eulogy while still alive, it’s on his memorial stone: “I died, but mafia is immortal”. So, when Putin became Sobchak’s curator from the KGB, he connected the city administration not only with the secret services but also with the organized crime, which mushroomed in 1990s on the ruins of the USSR. St. Petersburg’s administration was given the right to issue licenses on sales of the state resources (oil, precious and rare metals, etc.) and after the sales to foreign buyers went through, USD $122 million from these deals went missing. One of the first mentions of Vladimir Putin in the media was about these shady deals, which robbed St. Petersburg of the money needed to purchase food for the people — there were queues for bread in Russia at the time. There were many murders at the time in St. Petersburg with criminals and nouveau riches dividing the spheres of influence — and the KGB wasn’t uninvolved. In fact, the KGB used criminals to get control over money and assets — and then got rid of the criminal bosses after Putin’s accession to power in 2000. Krasikov is a privy to the wealth of secrets from these times — and likely the assassin behind many political liquidations on Putin’s direct orders, including the mysterious death of Putin’s former boss Anatoly Sobchak in February 2000 — weeks before Putin’s election as the President of Russia. Putin cannot afford the West to hold a key witness against him in a Hague trial — such secrets, if revealed, could mean the end of his legitimacy as the president of Russia in the eyes of the countries of “the global South” that still support him. That’s why Putin was willing to release 12 Russian political prisoners in exchange for Krasikov.

Why do you think the Russian government has refused to open a criminal investigation into the death of Alexei Navalny? The Russian state officially announced they wouldn’t be investigating the death of oppositionist Alexei Navalny — naturally, the FSB doesn’t want anyone near the obvious murder case, implicating Putin’s regime. Apparently, Navalny became unwell during his morning walk. He complained of a sharp stomach pain. He was taken back to the solo punishment cell by the guards, where he was thrown for some “violation”. It was the 27th time Navalny was in a solo punishment cell, usually this would be a 14-day punishment. He was found unresponsive in his cell later by guards and taken to medical quarters, an ambulance was called, but couldn’t revive him. A day before his death Navalny participated in a video hearing of his complaint and was in good spirits, appearing healthy. 2 days before his death, his parents visited him in prison, and also reported he was feeling well. The details on the actual circumstances of Navalny’s death were apparently reported by some guards or other prisoners through connections that his friend, investigator Christo Grozev, and other anti-Putin Russians in exile have within the Russian prison system. The papers provided by the Russian investigative committee, refusing to investigate causes of death, say that Navalny was taken to the medics from the walk. The official document also doesn’t mention Navalny’s complaint about the sharp stomach pain. Death was recorded at 2:17 pm. The time of death was recorded at that time, which is already fake, as he had likely died in the cell — he was unconscious when taken to the medical quarters. ”He was dying alone,” said Navalny’s widow Yulia. The cause of death is listed as “the combination of several illnesses”, and the main cause as “arrhythmia” (which is unidentifiable posthumously and never previously was diagnosed). Looks like Navalny might have been poisoned by an unknown toxin. Which probably will be never found, because the family agreed to bury the body. It’s 6 months since the death of Alexei Navalny. The team of investigators, linked to his exiled colleagues, still didn’t post anything conclusive about the causes of his death, but it’s possible they know much more than what his widow Yulia Navalnaya revealed in her yesterday’s video. It’s possible they even know the names of those FSB officers who visited the prison at the time, tasked to kill Navalny.

What do Russians think about Putin's wartime policies? Dmitry Grinchiy was born in the infamous year 1937 — the year of Stalin’s ‘Great Purge’. Just a few months after little Dmitry was born, his father Pavel Grinchiy was arrested by the NKVD. In 1938, Pavel Grinchiy was shot as ‘the enemy of the people.’ Just like a million of other Soviet citizens were shot. At the time, the Soviet people zealously supported the fight against "enemies of the people." Stalin’s propagandists repeated every day that “enemies and spies are everywhere”, and that “we must remain vigilant.” And the Soviet people were vigilant. They wrote millions of reports to the NKVD, pointing out potential “enemies of the people”. In all probabilities, Pavel Grinchiy was shot because someone he knew reported on him. 87 years have passed. Dmitry Grinchiy (who never even got to know his own father, killed on Stalin’s orders), lived his life in the USSR — through the collapse of the USSR, through “terrible 1990s” and the 25 years of Putin’s regime, from its inception to the fated launch of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In 2024, he found himself in a country where the regime every day tells the citizens that “enemies and spies are everywhere” and that “we must be vigilant”. And the Russian people are vigilant. Yesterday, 2 such vigilant Russian citizens attacked Dmitry Grinchiy on a bus in Moscow, they beat him up and dragged him to a police station. (Video in the comments below.) The 2 vigilantes decided that Grinchiy was “an enemy of the people” simply because (in their view) Grinchy said something “disrespectful” about the monument to “Wagner” — the chief of which, Yevgeny Prigozhin, was, by the way, killed on Putin’s orders after an attempt of armed rebellion. Some say that the recent incursion by the Ukrainian forces may lead to another “Justice March” towards Moscow. Fortunately for Grinchiy, the police decided to release him. Maybe because they didn’t want to lock up the old man immediately — the Russian prosecution machine has a habit of charging and locking up people after some time, even though initially the accused have been released after being detained and questioned. It’s unlikely the vigilantes will get as much as a slap in the wrist, after beating the old man. I’m shocked how quickly — in front of my eyes — Russia turned from a country pretending to be a semi-liberal democracy into a full-blown militaristic dictatorship, where people write reports on friends and family for “saying wrong things”, where books are being burned, with non-stop hateful propaganda from every screen. I’m shocked — but the majority of Russians are earnestly embracing “the new realities” with vigor and dedication not seen since 1937.

What do you make of the fact that Paul Whelan was left out of the prisoner exchange between the US and Russia? In December 2022, Paul Whelan wasn’t part of a prisoner exchange between Russia and the U.S. — instead, American basketball player Brittney Greener was traded for Russian arms dealer Victor Bout. Since then, there weren’t exchanges that were made public. Exchanges are never straightforward and who gets back is determined not only by what one side desires but also whom the opposition is prepared to exchange. Victor Bout, Brittney Griner. Putin managed to get his “merchant of death” Bout back, releasing an American hostage Griner who was arrested in Russia for carrying vaporizer cartridges containing less than a gram of hash oil. Russia accused her in possession of illegal drugs and sentenced for 9 years of prison. While possessing marijuana is illegal in Russia, the whole arrest and sentencing of Griner were handled with such media frenzy and promotion by Russian propagandists and the Kremlin bots online that it looked like a special operation to pressure the American side to release a well-connected arms dealer — by the end of 2022, Putin desperately needed someone experienced in that particular sector. Why Paul Whelan wasn’t exchanged at the time was asked by many, and the answer is that maybe Russia wanted someone else in exchange to Whelan whom the FSB insists was a real spy. Security professional Paul Whelan was arrested in Moscow in 2018 and accused of being a spy. Whelan said he had been in Russia for a friend's wedding. Before 2008, Whelan served as a Marine, and after his discharge was working as a security chief for a commercial organization. He visited Russia several times before and the wedding he was planning to attend was of a fellow marine. Whelan says he was given the hard drive by a Russian friend in what he now he now believes was a “sting operation” — Russia accused the drive contained some classified intel and sentenced him to 16 years imprisonment. This week, after several Russian political prisoners disappeared from their prisons in Russia, it was discovered that Paul Whelan is also missing. So are Putin’s critics journalist Maria Ponomarenko and an opposition politician Vladimir Kara-Murza. More confirmations are coming from Russia that a big prisoner exchange deal is in the works. Maybe this time Paul Whelan will also be released.

Can Ukraine make its own weapons? Ukraine can and does make its own weapons: Russia-Ukraine war of 2022–2024 is the first war in history where drones became the weapons that dominate the terrain. Within the last 2 years, drone production in Ukraine grew 100-fold. Since February 2022, Ukraine created and developed the UAV market from the ground up. One of such manufacturers are making drones called “Hornets”. There are smaller and larger FPV drones — “Wild Hornets”, “Queen Hornets”, as well as other models. All of them are Ukrainian-made. The Ukrainian drone operators have learned to use the same drone for many missions — a drone drops explosives and returns to the base, to get munitions. Drones are even used to retrieve weapons from the battlefield. Here you can see “Hornet Queen” picking weapons on the battlefield using a magnet. In December 2023, Ukraine’s President Zelenskyy set the task of producing a million drones for the Ukrainian Armed Forces. By now, the task has been completed, says Ukraine’s minister of digital transformation Mykhailo Fedorov. There are already contracts for the production of a million of drones for the Ukrainian army. They include standard FPV drones, long-range, reconnaissance and other types of drones that are already used by the Ukrainian defenders at the front. Just imagine this number: 1,000,000 drones! It’s 2 drones per each Russian soldier on the Ukrainian land. But tens of thousands of drones go directly from manufacturers to the Ukrainian units at the front without involving the government and the ministry of defense. They are paid for from donations that people make on behalf of certain units. So, if a certain unit requires more drones, they place a request with a manufacturer they know, and get a delivery within days, without the need for ministerial approvals. This is why the Ukrainian army is so much more efficient, and why the Russian soldiers say that it feels like the Ukrainians have 50:1 advantage in drones. This also saves thousands of Ukrainian lives.

Has Putin already decided to attack NATO? Putin can’t attack NATO countries while he’s stuck in the war of attrition in Ukraine. But if Putin is allowed to take over Ukraine — or “freeze” the war on current separation lines, with Ukraine being forced to de-arm and the ability of Russia to mobilize soldiers from the occupied Ukrainian territories (which they already do), then the chance of Putin attacking Baltics increases tenfold. And vice versus, if Russia is decisively defeated in Ukraine, the threat of Putin attacking a NATO country in Europe will drop close to 0%. Russia will not be able to recover quickly and Europe will have enough time to prepare an impenetrable defense. Putin won’t have the resources to attack the Baltic countries or Poland, if he suffers defeat and his army is destroyed in Ukraine. That’s why the most logical course of action for the European allies of Ukraine is to send Ukrainians enough weapons to destroy Putin’s army in Ukraine, so he cannot even think about an attack on Europe. Then these weapons that are stored in the warehouses won’t be needed in the future.

What role did the European Union play in the collapse of the Soviet Union, besides economic factors? The Maastricht Treaty that laid down the foundation for the European Union was signed in 1992 and went into effect in 1993. The Belovezha Accords that resulted in dissolution of the Soviet Union were signed in 1991. The desire of the first Russia’s president Boris Yeltsin to take full control of the whole of Russia, without having to report to the Union state and the USSR president Gorbachev, was the main driver of that move. 3 presidents — of Belarus, Russia and Ukraine — signed the Belovezha accords on December 8, 1991. They actually were supposed to negotiate a new Confederation deal between the republics, to reenergize the Soviet Union, but the 3 presidents chose to destroy it instead. The European Union had nothing to do with it. It was pure greed and lust for power of the first elected leader of Russia.

What will happen if Russia runs out of manpower for the military? August 2024: Russian soldiers surrender en masse in the Kursk region of Russia, overpowered and outnumbered by the Ukrainian forces in their own territory. How the tables have turned: The photos of the annihilated Russian column that was bringing soldiers to the front in the Kursk region are all over the Russian social networks. The Russian correspondents first showed the column moving through the Kursk region, and then other Russians filmed it burning and the aftermath of the attack. The FSB arrested a man who filmed the burning trucks and made him confess that he was doing it on orders of the Ukrainians. Someone has to be blamed for the major security screw up! Could this be true? Russian newspaper: 17,000 Wagner soldiers from prisons killed on the battlefield. What do people in Russia know about this? Is the truth hidden for Russians? From July 1, 2022 to February 7, 2023, Yevgeny Prigozhin’s ‘Wagner’ recruited 48,366 prisoners; 17,251 of them were killed in Ukraine, reported oppositional Russian media outlet ‘Mediazona’. These losses exceed the total number of killed in action during the 10 years of the USSR invasion of Afghanistan. Most fighters recruited by ‘Wagner’ from prisons were sent into “meat assaults” near Bakhmut — and 17,000 of them died there. the Battle of Bakhmut lasted 327 days, from July 15, 2022, till June 6, 2023. During this time: 35% of recruited prisoners (1 in 3) died. In the Battle of Bakhmut, Russian forces captured 677 sq. km of territory(261 square miles). 29 dead soldiers for each 1 square km. When recruiting inmates in prisons, Yevgeny Prigozhin told them that they would’t be just “cannon fodder”, but would serve as equals with the other mercenaries. But the casualties data show that it wasn’t the case: the share of “free mercenaries” among these killed in action is only 12%. Before the start of the Battle of Bakhmut and recruiting in prisons (March-June 2022), Wagner lost only 300 men. ’Mediazona’ determined the number of deaths by the records of payments to families of the deceased. (The journalists got hold of Wagner’s financial documentation, and then cross-referenced it with databases on inheritance, presidential pardons, court verdicts, etc.) ‘Wagner’ recruiters went through 617 Russian prisons and penal colonies, where they recruited over 48,000 convicted criminals. The majority of them were pulled from maximum security prisons. After the aborted ‘Wagner’ coup in June 2023, Russian authorities tried to bury ‘Wagner’ into oblivion. But “meat assault” tactics, first used in Ukraine by Prigozhin, are now implemented by regular Russian infantry units, as well as units made of inmates. To compare, the project UALosses, which calculates military losses by Ukraine, recorded that 4,871 Ukrainians (confirmed with names) were killed in the Battle of Bakhmut from July 15, 2022 to June 6, 2023. (The actual number is likely higher, up to 8,000.) But there were not only ‘Wagner’ mercenaries involved in the operation in Bakhmut, regular Russian troops had been there as well. So, proportionately, Russian losses are likely to be no less than 3:1 in Bakhmut, or higher. But it doesn’t seem that losses among prisoners — or even deaths of Russia’s contract soldiers or mobilized — are a worry for the Russian populace. Putin’s propaganda machine turned into a death cult where perishing in the war of conquest in the name of “Great Russia” is publicly glorified — while no one actually cares about the disabled vets or families who lost fathers, husbands, and sons. Most Russians don’t care — as long as they can keep living their lives, pretending that nothing happens.

Are there any specific stories within the 100 Ukrainians released from Russian captivity that you found particularly moving? Here is this story that I cried reading. You might cry, too. A guy tells his mother after being released from captivity: “We didn’t believe in the exchange until the very end. Because they deceived us so much, they tormented us... They would take us for executions and for exchanges... And then they would bring us back and laugh at us. And when a soldier came into the bus and said, "You’re home, boys, Glory to Ukraine!" - I just started breathing; I hadn't been breathing, Mom, really. And when we saw people along the road greeting us with flags, flowers, and signs, it felt like a movie, like it wasn’t happening to us. And then, when we finally arrived, the first cigarette, hugs, they gave us a phone, I forgot your number, Mom, can you imagine? But you’re not mad, because how could I forget your number? I repeated it to myself for 2 years. Like you taught me in childhood - "My name is...., I live at..., Mom’s phone number is...." The boys cried, but I didn't. And at the hospital, they gave us clothes and took us to the dining room. And there was food, Mom. There were 3 bowls of different things for each of us. I don’t know, I didn’t eat that much in captivity in a month. And the smell of the soup. My head started spinning. The bowl was so deep, the soup was up to the brim. I was so careful with the spoon, trying not to spill anything, but my hands were shaking, Mom, because I wanted to eat properly, but I also wanted to just grab the bowl and drink it all. And my hands were shaking. And oh, how much I wanted to eat, you can’t imagine. And I was so careful, trying to be proper... A lady walked around, refilling everything for us, she came up to me, hugged me, stroked my head like Grandma used to, kissed me on the temple - "Eat, dear, I’ll bring more," she said. And that’s when I cried. I ate and cried, afraid to look up because I felt ashamed. And then I looked around, and almost all of us were like that - eating and crying. And the soup, Mom, I’ve never had anything tastier in my life. You’re not upset, are you, Mom?”
