Russia has a history of throwing its citizens under the military wheel. What happens when the butcher's bill is too much for ordinary Russians? What happens when they realise, that in 2024, they don't have to die for a lunatic with an ego problem? A Russian deserter who was tricked to sign up for the war told ‘The Insider’ how he was nearly killed by his own Russian troops at the front, next to a pit with 20–30 bodies. He was badly wounded when his commander sent him to pick some vodka, and nearly bled out with no assistance. It was after this experience that he decided to run off. Anton (not his real name) had no intention of joining the army whatsoever. But in the fall of 2023, he went out to a shop, and a police patrol stopped him to check his documents. Anton didn’t have his ID with him and the cops took him to the police station. They put his data into a computer and told him he had an outstanding mobilization summons and would be going to the front in 3 days. They threatened that he would have huge problems for trying to skip mobilization — but there could be a way around: he could go to the enlistment office and ask to sign the contract voluntarily. The cops told him that if he signed the contract (as opposed to being mobilized), he would be able to pick an “easy” job, like helping out in a hospital. Anton came home horrified. The idea of improving his odds to get an “easy” military job as opposed to being sent to the front as mobilized seemed reasonable. He decided that if he anyway would be mobilized, he’d better become a contractor. He signed the contract on Saturday, and on Tuesday he was already sent to a unit. And — surprise, surprise! — he was sent to an assault company. A week later he was already at the front line. That was a shock for Anton: “A week ago I was sitting at home, watching videos, working, leading a normal life, and now I'm at the trenches in Ukraine.” It didn’t take long at the front for commanders to start sending people to assaults. His unit’s goal was to take a position at the edge of a village. But to get there, the soldiers had to run over 500 meters of an open space. From the Ukrainian side, that open space was controlled by a machine gun that was able to take out up to 100 people at once. The only cover a group could take was a damaged tank stranded in the middle. The commander told the assault teams to take cover and dig an outpost near the tank, to create a position from which they would be able to move further forward. Anton says it was an idiotic plan: there was no difference whether you had to run 250 or 500 meters, after 30 seconds in an open area you would be a “toast”. The commander began sending groups of 5: on the first day, 4 groups were sent, all 20 ended up dead. No one could even reach that tank. The next day another 20 people got killed. Anton says, Ukrainians have 15–20 various drones — both killer drones and reconnaissance drones — in the air at any time, day or night. The drones see any movement immediately. “It felt like the Ukrainian Armed Forces had a 50-fold advantage in drones,” he says. Then the commanders decided to send only 2 people at once. One group managed to reach the tank and dug in, and the propagandists on TV immediately began reporting that “the village was taken.” But the Russian troops still haven’t even reached it. The commander, a former security guard from a supermarket, dreamed of seeing himself on Channel 1, to feel like a hero warrior. So, he kept sending one group after the other to the slaughter, demanding that they move forward towards the village. The group that dug in near the tank managed to survive, but they needed ammunition, food, water — so, more people were sent in to deliver supplies, and they kept being shot by the Ukrainian fire. Anton says that about 70 people died there in a week, near that tank. Anton says that the worst wasn’t even the gunfire — the worst was when you leave the dugout and are completely exposed, and you realize that at any second you can be killed. “I went out to the toilet, went back 30 seconds later, and at the place where I was, 2 mortars hit” he recalls. Sometimes the Ukrainian drone operators made errors and the drones fell down, then the commanders sent Russian soldiers into the minefields to pick them up. A task from which one is unlikely to return, because no one has maps of the minefields, the mines are just thrown in, where it falls, that’s where it falls. “You have a patch of land, 4 drones fly around it. They drop something, as soon as they fly away — the next 4 are already flying. And in the distance, there are probably 5 more, coordinating fire by mortars and artillery,” explains Anton. If a drone noticed you, you aren’t allowed to hide back in a dugout — because the operator sees a glowing dot, and suddenly it disappears: it means the person has gone somewhere. Then a precise hit arrives — and minimum 5 people in the dugout will be dead. Anton says that in 2 weeks, only 15–20 people were left from 250 soldiers that arrived, and from them 10 people were the commanders and non-combat clerks. Most of the soldiers were contractors, only a few were “mobilized”. From the losses, about 40% are dead, the rest are wounded. About 50% of the wounded are without legs or arms — disabled for life. “When I arrived, that village was still more or less intact. 3 weeks later it was just ruins. Heaps of corpses…” recalls Anton. He survived because he was part of the “evacuation team” — and he refused to go in the assaults, saying he would continue performing the task he was assigned to do. He was still going to the position near the tank, but his job was to pull the wounded, not carry provisions or stay in the dugout. Although Anton didn’t do any specific medical training, he had to perform an amputation in the field. This was like a horror movie. He pulled a guy who was lying wounded in the field for 3 days. The guy managed to apply tourniquets to wounds on his arm and leg, but after these 3 days his arm began to rot. The medics told him on the radio he had to amputate the arm. Anton injected the guy with all sedatives he could find and chopped the arm with an axe. It took him 4 attempts to get through the flesh and bones, then he had to treat the stump and bandage it. “I didn't sleep for two days after that,” Anton says. “When we were loading him [for evacuation], he was still alive, and he also made it to the first line alive. I don't know what happened to him after that.” Another guy that Anton pulled out had part of his jaw torn off, his arm up to the shoulder and half a leg. The commander was pissed off about it: "I don't need this, now I have to do something for one more person." A day later the injured guy was already begging to die, realizing he wouldn’t survive. At the end, he bled to death. The dead were rarely pulled out from the field. It was too much trouble to even attempt it. Once Anton had to hide from a drone and crawled into an old dugout, and realized he was crawling on top of liquified bodies in uniform. The bodies were there for already 3–4 months. There was one guy in the unit of about 18–19, he was a draftee (all Russian men have to serve a 1-year compulsory military service, but the draftees are not supposed to be sent to Ukraine to the war). That guy was also tricked into signing a contract — in the military enlistment office where he arrived as a draftee, they simply gave him some papers to sign, and he signed, not realizing what it was. “A week and a half later, he was already at the front line,” says Anton. The guy’s family sent a letter, complaining to the prosecutor's office that he was forced to sign the contract. The battalion commander was furious about it and gave the order to “sort him out.” The teenage soldier was sent into an attack and killed within a week. Anton says his commander was constantly drunk. One day the commander ordered him to pick another drone from the headquarters — Anton argued it was unnecessary to do it at night, as they had a spare drone they could use, and at night it’s really easy to see a person on thermal visors. But the commander insisted. Anton managed to get to the headquarters, where they gave him a drone and a package “for the commander”. Anton looked inside the bag, and there were bottles of vodka and cognac. The commander sent him to get the alcohol for him and he didn’t care it was deadly dangerous. On the way back, Anton heard a drone over him and immediately an explosive dropped on him. Anton was wounded and couldn’t walk, but he realized he still had both his arms and legs. He threw away the bag with vodka and crawled into the nearest basement, got on the radio, said that he was wounded and asked for evacuation. They responded it was too dangerous to try to get him. After 20 minutes, he realized that he was bleeding out. “I was shaking all over, tremors, I definitely lost a liter of blood,” says Anton. He decided to crawl, and managed to make it to the line where he could be picked up — out of the firing range. Anton says that ”almost everyone drinks” at the front line — or they are using cheap drugs (“salts”). The commanders also steal strong pain killers from the first aid kits given to soldiers and use those. If a soldier refuses to follow orders, he isn’t sent to a military court for prosecution but simply shot by the commander’s underlings — his arms and legs are taped to a tree, and he’s shot at a point blank range. Sometimes a person may be dressed in 2 bulletproof vests and then shot at with a machine gun, his ribs get broken and he slowly dies. Or he’s shot at through a helmet — such shots take off the whole skull. Anton says that 2 soldiers in his unit were liquidated like this, for not following orders — they refused to go in an attack, because all previous groups were killed. Anton himself nearly got shot — when in the field, he noticed a drone in the sky and went back, but took to the left and ended up in a neighboring unit. That unit was looking for a mobilized soldier on the run and took Anton for the deserter. He was tied to a tree and about to be shot, there was a hole nearby, where 20–30 bodies were already lying. He was saved by a radio message that the runaway soldier was found. Do the Russian soldiers realize that Russia’s war in Ukraine is evil? Do they blame Putin for that? Nobody among the Russian troops at the front says things like "let's go overthrow Putin,” states Anton. “Of course, they say that he [Putin] has started some kind of screwup that no one needs.” ”Even the ‘patriots’ when they arrive, very soon start saying, ‘What are we even doing here, why the heck do we need this?’” “There are some ‘ultra patriots’, but they do not survive for long, because they are the first to run ahead and the first to get killed.” “There was this guy, 54 years old, his wife had cancer. He came not even for the money, but because he needed the benefits for a serviceman's family, so his wife could get the cancer treatment. He was saying: ‘I know that people get killed here, I made my choice. If I get killed, at least my wife will get 5 million ruble, she will get the treatment, the children will live well." That guy lived in a small regional town. His monthly salary was 35,000 ruble (about USD$400). He had 3 kids, his wife was sick. He saw it as his only option to help the wife and the kids. “You are not a human being there at all,” says Anton. He fears what is going to happen in Russia when all these people with the broken psyche come back. “When these people come back from the war with blood on their hands, with a broken psyche, who were in the same companies, detachments and so on, they will start to form groups, and these smaller groups will start to form bigger groups...” Anton says that plenty of weapons are transported back to Russia in bags with dead bodies — pulled into parts and hidden in these bags. An AK-47 costs about 40,000 ruble in Russia now ($460). Anton says that if the Russian soldiers are being utilized at the same rate as at his part of the front, Russia has suffered about 400,000 losses by now — killed and badly wounded. Anton says that no one signing an army contract should hope they’d come back with the money — because they won’t. At best, they can hope to come back home with the money in case of a serious wound — but then, “Do you want your mother to be wiping off your butt for the rest of your life?” “If you think there are some Nazis there... There are no Nazis, there are ordinary people. If you, so to say, go and kill your neighbor, would you be able to live with that for the rest of your life?” “This war is not worth it. This is not a war for the Fatherland, this is not a war for justice, not a war for freedom — this is a war for the complete bullshit. A war for the grandfather who is so crazy that he went and killed hundreds of thousands of people for nothing, just like that.” “You are not liberating anyone. He [the crazy grandfather] himself doesn't believe that he is liberating anyone, he doesn't give a f**k about all this — and even less about you.” What can the Russian men do to avoid being sent to the war? “Better run,” says Anton. ”No money? Take out loans and use that money to escape.” Anton himself deserted after getting wounded. Yesterday, Putin signed a decree raising the federal payout on signing the army contact to 400,000 rub. ($4,600) — it’s nearly twice as much as the state was paying before. Regions are also raising their payouts — St. Petersburg just raised it’s top-up to 1.8 million, and Moscow already lifted it to 1.9 million rub. ($22,000). Russia is running out of volunteers, so the prices for cannon fodder are rising. Putin is too scared to do another mobilization and force people to kill and die, because he knows how unpopular this war really is.

When will Putin stop? If Putin were locked in a prison cell, this madness of a full-scale war in Ukraine and constant Russian threats would certainly stop. Failing that (which would be only possible through an internal coup), Putin would be forced to stop if he could no longer draft enough soldiers to send to the war in Ukraine or was unable to equip them with weapons. Willingly, Putin might stop if he were given an appearance of a victory in Ukraine: something that he could announce to the Russian populace as a triumph. For 2.5 years of the full-scale war, the Russian populace had been diligently suppressed to the level where they don’t dare to speak up — they can’t even verbalize their dismay with being “best friends” with the North Korea, which for decades has been the butt of every joke about backward dictatorships. The Russian people have to swallow their nationalistic chauvinism and display satisfaction about “strategic alliance” of Putin and Kim Jong Un. Despite numerous failures in Ukraine, Putin’s propaganda still claims that Putin is “winning” — and that they “haven’t really started yet”, and the Russian population accepts it as the indisputable truth. So, whatever Putin decides to announce as a “victory” in Ukraine, wouldn’t be disputed by the population — no matter how shameful the conditions of the deal would be for Russia. Putin’s refusal to give up isn’t because of him being afraid to lose power — it’s purely an obsession. Putin made a mistake and refuses to admit it, pretending “all is going according to plan”. Alas, the likelihood of Putin’s getting to his senses and starting to make decisions that are rational (i.e. good for Russia and Russians) isn’t high. Most likely, he would do anything to continue the war in Ukraine, hoping he’d have a chance to prevail if his army were able to last another few months — ad nauseam. Meanwhile, Russia’s economy is in deep trouble, which even the Russian officials can no longer deny. In words of the first deputy chairman of the Central Bank Vladimir Chistyukhin, the system is on the brink of a “collapse”, because of Russia’s incorrigible dependency on import. In other words, if Russia can’t import goods and services, its economy would crash within months. The latest western sanctions severely impacted Russia’s ability to pay for imported goods via legitimate payment methods, and the Russian Central Bank is unable to bypass this block, desperately researching crutch options, including barter and use of cryptocurrencies. Putin is willing to bet Russia’s present and future on his neo-USSR project. And he is convinced that Ukraine is ‘the Holy Grail’ that would tip the scales in his favor. But for that, he needs the whole of Ukraine — he can’t allow any part of Ukraine, especially Kyiv, to stay out of his grasp. He needs Odesa, he needs Mykolaiv, he needs Kharkiv. He can’t get it by force — not for the lack of trying. Putin is prepared to try to get it by other means, and his preference would be to turn Ukrainians against their government, to instigate an “anti-Maidan” coup, and install a puppet government to rule over Ukraine. That in his view is the most promising and cost effective course of action, and that’s why anyone in the west willing to sell out to Russia gets paid handsomely — Jason Hinkle recently bragged he bought a plane from his earnings on X-Twitter: Kremlin bots promote threads through incessant commenting and reposts, and Musk pays out the cash. Simple scheme. Just remember: Putin’s goal is the destroy the USA, EU and NATO. Even if the war in Ukraine stops, Putin won’t stop the war against the West. Only a change of regime in Russia can stop it.
